Prior to this position, Mr. Beck served as the Vice President of Strategic Initiatives for Consolidated Nuclear Security, LLC (CNS), which is responsible for the management and operation of the Y-12 National Security Complex in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. In this position, he oversaw strategic opportunities and planning for the company. At CNS, Mr. Beck also served as Vice President of Program Integration—providing planning, budgeting, and program management to CNS as it managed and operated the Pantex Plant in Amarillo, Texas, and Y-12. Dave Chisenhall Dave Chisenhall serves as the acting director of Business Operations for the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Legacy Management (LM). He provides executive leadership and oversight of the organization’s business operations, supporting LM’s mission through strategic planning, operational excellence, organizational performance, and responsible stewardship of public resources. As director, Chisenhall leads the business operations that enable mission execution across LM’s nationwide portfolio. He oversees business process improvement, enterprise modernization, executive decision support, organizational planning, performance management, and resource management. Chisenhall works closely with DOE senior leadership to strengthen organizational effectiveness, improve operational performance, and advance the Department’s strategic priorities. Chisenhall has more than 34 years of experience in program, construction, and project management in the federal government. He brings 20 years of experience in both public and private sector capacity including counter-threat finance with the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), and in the small business international procurement and supply chain industry, supporting U.S. embassy logistical operations around the globe. Mr. Bolls consulted at Booz Allen Hamilton, and also coordinated fact checking for Presidential speeches on defense affairs for the White House. At DIA, he facilitated public-private partnerships bringing corporate best practices into federal government and served as liaison with allied foreign partner nations. Mr. Bolls studied at Grove City College and the graduate Institute for World Politics. He is a volunteer for the Emergency Response Virginia Defense Force, which collaborates with the National Guard and FEMA on disaster prevention and recovery.

pages.title: David Bushnell's 'Turtle' Was the World's First Combat Submarine
pages.description: David Bushnell developed the "Turtle" submersible as a student at Yale University. The vessel's attack on a British flagship failed, but the trailblazing boat's legacy endures 250 years later
pages.text: David Bushnell's 'Turtle' Was the World's First Combat Submarine Skip to main content America's 250th Anniversary A Smithsonian magazine special report A diagram of David Bushnell's Turtle submersible Library of Congress Prints and Photographs Division During the American Revolution, the Turtle made history as the world’s first combat-ready submarine. If all went according to plan, the driver of the acorn-shaped submersible—constructed out of oak and iron hoops—would descend, draw close enough to a warship to attach a bomb to its hull and then make their escape by ascending to the surface. Connecticut inventor David Bushnell designed the Turtle as a secret weapon for the patriots to wield against the British. Nearly 250 years ago, on the night of September 6-7, 1776, the vessel targeted the Royal Navy’s flagship, the HMS Eagle —and failed. In the centuries since, however, the story of the souped-up submersible that went up against the greatest navy in the world has served as a testament to the revolutionary spirit. Bushnell started experimenting with gunpowder while enrolled at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut. He knew that a bomb affixed to a ship’s hull would inflict more damage than one placed on its deck. First, he had to figure out how to get explosives to work underwater. Then he would turn to the question of how to transport the device. Mr. Denton brings more than 20 years of experience in executive leadership, engineering, and infrastructure development. Prior to joining OE, he held senior leadership positions with the U.S. Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Reclamation, where he led an organization of more than 600 employees. His career also includes overseeing major energy and infrastructure projects at the Department of Energy’s Hanford Site and leading complex hydropower initiatives across the Northwest. Over a 14-year career, Wright appeared in around 56 percent as many games as Baines, resulting in 1,089 fewer hits and 142 fewer home runs. But what Wright did each time he took the field was statistically more impactful. As measured by WAR , Wright’s five best seasons were all better than Baines’ best. In terms of league-adjusted OPS+ , Wright had three campaigns at least as good as Baines’ top year. The top moments of David Wright's career In the seasons in which he appeared in at least 110 games, Wright made the All-Star Game 78 percent of the time. Baines’ rate was 35 percent. Baines never finished higher than ninth in MVP voting. Wright was ninth or better four times. In this role, she leads DOE’s enterprise information technology and cybersecurity initiatives, ensuring that DOE’s systems are secure, efficient, and innovative. Dawn plays a pivotal role in aligning DOE’s IT modernization efforts with its broader mission priorities, including transformative technology programs that advance U.S. energy security and innovation. With over 25 years of experience and a proven track record of excellence across government, academia, and the private sector, Ms. Zimmer brings a deep understanding of how to build and sustain high-performing technology organizations. pages.text: Death of a Family Member | U.S. Department of Labor Skip to main content Death of a Family Member When an employee covered under an employer-sponsored health plan dies, the covered spouse and dependent children need to consider their options for health coverage. If the spouse has an employer health plan available at work, the spouse and any dependents may be eligible to special enroll in that plan. Or, they may be able to special enroll in health coverage through the Marketplace. The spouse and any dependent children also may be eligible to continue their existing health coverage for up to 36 months. The plan should notify them of their right to purchase extended health care coverage under COBRA. Most plans require eligible individuals to make their COBRA election of coverage within 60 days of the plan's notice. The premature death of a spouse can undermine efforts for the partner to save for retirement, particularly if there are dependent children. That's why it's important to check your Social Security statement to find out how much children will receive if a parent dies. Maintaining adequate life insurance is also important. Be sure that you have properly named the beneficiaries for any insurance policies, retirement plans, IRAs, and other retirement vehicles. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Decades-long Access Issue Resolved at Pike Ridge Near Rangely Nov 5, 2026 RANGELY, Colo. – For more than 40 years, a locked gate at the end of Rio Blanco County Road 27 complicated public access to thousands of acres of Bureau of Land Management land south of Rangely. Hunters, anglers and other visitors could reach the area on foot, but the nearest available parking was nearly two miles away. A locked gate along Rio Blanco County Road 27 restricted vehicle access to BLM-managed public lands near Pike Ridge for more than 40 years. The gate was removed in October 2025 after a BLM investigation confirmed the road's status as a county road. That changed last fall when the gate was removed, reopening vehicle access for the first time since the 1980s. Now, a partnership between the BLM White River Field Office and Rio Blanco County has completed improvements that make it easier for visitors to reach Pike Ridge while protecting the area's natural resources. The law also requires the U.S. Census Bureau to furnish tabulations of population to each state, including for those small areas the states have identified, within one year of Census day. Since the first Census Redistricting Data Program, conducted as part of the 1980 census, the U.S. Census Bureau has included summaries for the major race groups specified by the Statistical Programs and Standards Office of the U.S. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in Directive 15 (as issued in 1977 and revised in 1997). Originally, the tabulation groups included White, Black, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Asian/Pacific Islander, plus “some other race.” These race data were also cross-tabulated by Hispanic/Non-Hispanic origin. At the request of the state legislatures and the Department of Justice, for the 1990 Census Redistricting Data Program, voting age (18 years old and over) was added to the cross-tabulation of race and Hispanic origin. During your research, you may come across "withdrawal notices" or forms that indicate a record is restricted and not available to the public. This process provides continuous protection of classified records ensures the accessibility to records of historic value and helps maintain the public trust by providing public accountability. NARA has several roles concerning declassification and the handling of restricted records. We process, withdraw and store sensitive documents, maintain a classified database, create labels and consults with on-site reviewers from agencies. NARA also processes FOIA requests and the Director of Information Security Oversight Office ( ISOO ) serves as the Executive Secretary of the Interagency Security Classification Appeals Panel ( ISCAP ). pages.text: Decoded secret letters reveal royal plot against Queen Elizabeth I | National Geographic Premium HISTORY MAGAZINE Decoded secret letters reveal royal plot against Queen Elizabeth I The imprisoned Mary, Queen of Scots used sophisticated ciphers as she conspired to overthrow her cousin, Elizabeth I. Long thought lost, the letters were hiding in plain sight. A portrait of a bejeweled Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots, was painted by Henri Serrur in 1840. Versailles, Château De Versailles Photograph by DeAgostini, Getty Images By Kathryn Miles Published February 8, 2023 • 11 min read Mary, Queen of Scots, was a master at sending secret messages, and codebreakers have spent centuries frustrated by her sharp ciphering skills. Whenever her surviving exchanges have been cracked, scholars thrill to the information found inside. But the existence of one set of letters, believed lost, has tantalized historians for centuries: the ones she penned during her nineteen years in English prisons. Prior to her execution on February 8, 1587, Mary Stuart wrote dozens of secret letters to French officials believed to contain sensitive information about her plots to regain the Scottish throne and to usurp her first cousin and political rival, Queen Elizabeth I . For centuries, scholars thought these letters were either irretrievably hidden or destroyed, but an international trio of amateur codebreakers has just proven them wrong. pages.description: To see a “world of life almost as unknown as that of Mars,” two explorers climbed inside the bathysphere and descended into the sea’s cold depths in 1931.
pages.text: Deep underwater, sealed inside a metal ball, these explorers made history | National Geographic By William Beebe Last updated January 13, 2026 This story originally published in the June 1931 issue of National Geographic magazine. See more digitized stories from our archives here. Several years ago I climbed overboard into the clear waters of Haiti, and after a copper helmet had been lowered over my head and shoulders I slid slowly down a rope two, four, eight, ten fathoms and finally at sixty-three feet my canvas shoes settled into the soft ooze near a coral reef. I made my way to a steep precipice, balanced on the brink, and looked down, down into the green depths where illumination like moonlight showed waving sea-fans and milling fish far beyond the length of my hose. It would have been exceedingly unwise to go much farther, for the steady force of the weight of water at ten fathoms had already increased the pressure on eardrums and every portion of my head and body to almost forty-five pounds for each square inch. At double the depth I had reached I would probably become insensible and unable to ascend. How the bathysphere was conceived As I peered down I realized I was looking toward a world of life almost as unknown as that of Mars or Venus—a world in which, up to the present time, our efforts at capturing the inhabitants have been pitifully trivial. Credit: Michael Skrepnick SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Deinocheirus Exposed: Meet The Body Behind the Terrible Hand By Ed Yong Published October 22, 2014 • 7 min read The original “terrible hands”. Credit: Eduard Solà For 50 years, the dinosaur was just a pair of arms. But what arms! Each was eight feet (2.4 metres) long, and ended in three eight-inch (20-centimetre) claws. You can understand why the scientists who discovered this beast called it Deinocheirus mirificus , from the Greek for “terrible hand, which is unusual”. The arms, hands, and shoulder girdle were discovered in 1965 in Mongolia’s Gobi desert, nestled within a 70-million-year-old sandstone formation. But the rest of the skeleton was missing, save for a few uninformative fragments. Palaeontologists have repeatedly ventured into the Gobi to try and find the rest of the animal, but without success. These failures have turned Deinocheirus into one of palaeontology’s most enduring mysteries. What kind of dinosaur was it? It was big, but how big? What did it eat? How did it live? No one could say. It was a riddle, wrapped in an enigma, hidden behind two gigantic arms. pages.text: Demographic Analysis (DA) Demographic Analysis (DA) Skip Navigation Within About Demographic Analysis (DA) Demographic Analysis (DA) is a method used to evaluate the quality of the census. We use current and historical vital records, data on international migration, and Medicare records to produce national estimates of the population on April 1 by age, sex, the DA race categories, and Hispanic origin. The DA population estimates are independent of the decennial census. The results are used to produce estimates of net coverage error, which are calculated as the percent difference between the census counts and the DA population estimates. Traditionally, the DA estimates have been produced by sex and single year of age for the race categories Black and non-Black. Starting in 2010, the DA program produces estimates by Hispanic origin (Hispanic/Non-Hispanic) for a limited number of ages. pages.text: Dengue Skip to main content WHO/Karina Zambrana In Brazil, community health workers visit local residents to help find and destroy mosquito breeding sites. © Credits Dengue 21 August 2025 Reading time: Key facts Dengue is a viral infection caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected mosquitoes. About half of the world's population is now at risk of dengue, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year. Dengue is found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, mostly in urban and semi-urban areas. While many DENV infections are asymptomatic or produce only mild illness, DENV can occasionally cause more severe cases, and even death. Prevention and control of dengue rely on vector control. There is no specific treatment for dengue/severe dengue, and early detection and access to proper medical care greatly lower fatality rates of severe dengue. Overview Dengue (break-bone fever) is a viral infection that is spread from mosquitoes to people. It is more common in tropical and subtropical than in temperate climates. Most people who get dengue do not have symptoms. For those who do, the most common symptoms are high fever, headache, body aches, nausea and rash. Most get better in 1–2 weeks. Some develop severe dengue and need care in a hospital. In severe cases, dengue can be fatal. You can lower your risk of dengue by avoiding mosquito bites, especially during the day. Dengue Vaccines For Health Care Providers Sept. 1, 2026 Español Key points There are currently no dengue vaccines available in the United States. Globally, several dengue vaccines have been approved or are in different stages of development. People can continue to protect themselves and their families from dengue by preventing mosquito bites and controlling mosquitoes in and around their homes. Overview An ideal dengue vaccine would provide long-lasting protection against all four dengue viruses (DENV-1–4). People can get sick from dengue multiple times if they are infected by different dengue viruses. The dengue vaccines that have been evaluated to date have provided stronger protection in people who had a previous DENV infection compared to people without a previous DENV infection. The vaccines have also shown different levels of protection against the different DENVs. pages.text: Denisovan tooth found in Laos adds new wrinkles to their story | National Geographic The newfound tooth hails from Laos’s Cobra Cave—a cramped hollow embedded in a lush escarpment, as shown here. Scientists required a system of ropes to access the cave. Photograph by Fabrice Demeter SCIENCE Tooth from mysterious human relative adds new wrinkles to their story Discovered thousands of miles south of the only other known Denisovan fossils, the molar provides fresh evidence of the enigmatic humans’ spread across ancient Asia. By Maya Wei-Haas and Michael Greshko Published May 17, 2022 • 11 min read After scrambling up a steep rocky pitch in the Annamite Mountains of Laos, Laura Shackelford was initially underwhelmed. The paleoanthropologist from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign stood in a cramped hollow known as Cobra Cave, looking for bones that a local Hmong boy had mentioned seeing. Flipping on her flashlight, she swept the beam of light from one seemingly barren wall to another. Then she looked up. “I saw almost nothing but bone,” says Shackelford, who is also a National Geographic Explorer. Embedded in the rubbly ceiling were fossils of animals long gone, scattered across the cave’s roof “almost like stars.” For years Shackelford and her team had worked in Laos’s labyrinthine cave systems in search of ancient human remains, and she knew that this narrow passage was special. Photograph: Boliggaarden Denmark Denmark’s top court to rule on ‘parallel societies’ after ‘non-western’ people evicted Government claims removal of former residents of housing complex in Helsingør is unrelated to their ethnicity Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Fri 6 Nov 2026 05.00 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 06.42 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Denmark’s supreme court is expected to rule on whether the state’s classification of residents with “non-western” backgrounds is covered by racial discrimination law. The appeal by residents who were evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej in Helsingør, a city north of Copenhagen, could have far-reaching implications for others who have been forced out of their homes by the controversial legislation previously known as the “ghetto law”. The government now refers to affected neighbourhoods as “parallel societies”.
